articles.title: Aura Test: Find Out What Your Aura Color Says About You | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: Not sure what an aura test actually measures? Here's how aura color tests work, what each color means, and how to figure out yours without a special device.
articles.answer: An aura test is a way of identifying which color best represents your energy and personality, according to the New Age tradition of aura reading. There's no scientific instrument involved — the “test” is really a self-assessment: you compare your traits and current mood against the traditional meaning of each aura color.
sections: How aura tests actually work

Most online "aura tests" are one of two things: a short quiz that asks about your habits and preferences and maps your answers to a color, or a plain description of each color that you compare yourself against. Neither involves any equipment — despite some claims online, there's no camera or app that photographs an actual aura.
The value isn't in precision, it's in reflection: reading through the traits tied to each color is a quick way to think about your own personality and current state of mind.
The main aura colors and what they mean

ul: Blue — calm, communicative, a natural listener.
Yellow — optimistic, creative, mentally energetic.
Green — balanced, grounded, drawn to harmony.
White — going through (or seeking) a major transition.
Red — passionate, decisive, high physical energy.
Purple — intuitive, spiritual, a rare aura color.
Pink — affectionate, empathetic, relationship-focused.
Black — introspective, protective, often tied to a period of rest.

sections: Want the full breakdown for each one? The aura color test walks through the traits behind every color in more detail.
Can your aura color change?

According to the tradition, yes. Your aura color reflects your current state as much as your baseline personality, so it's normal to feel like you identify with a different color depending on what you're going through — or with two colors at once.
faq: Is there a real device that reads auras?

No verified scientific instrument measures an aura. Some “aura photography” booths use biofeedback sensors (like skin temperature) mapped to colors for entertainment, but this isn't a validated measurement of anything paranormal.
What's the difference between an aura test and an aura color test?
They're the same idea. This page is a general overview of how aura reading works; the aura color test goes deeper into the specific traits tied to each color.

articles.title: Piccolo Aura Farming: The Anime Edit Trend Explained | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: Why Piccolo became the face of aura farming edits, plus the other anime and game characters that get the same treatment: Gojo, Sung Jin Woo, Agamemnon.
articles.answer: Piccolo aura farming refers to a wave of edits that pair calm, understated moments of the Dragon Ball character Piccolo with epic music, framing his composure as maximum “aura” — the same social-media shorthand for effortless carisma that spawned the aura farming meme in the first place.
sections: Why Piccolo specifically

Aura farming edits are built on contrast: someone doing something impressive while looking completely unbothered. Piccolo fits that template almost perfectly — he's known for standing still, saying little, and rarely raising his voice even in high-stakes moments. Editors slow down or freeze-frame his stillest scenes, add a dramatic soundtrack, and the result reads as pure "aura" by the meme's own logic: no visible effort, no reaction, no explanation.
It also helps that Piccolo has decades of source material to pull from, so there's no shortage of clips that fit the format.
Gojo, Sung Jin Woo, and Agamemnon

Piccolo isn't alone. A handful of other characters get the same edit treatment for the same reason — each one has a signature "calm despite overwhelming power" moment that fits the aura farming template:

ul: Gojo Satoru (Jujutsu Kaisen) — his casual confidence and one-liners in the middle of fights make him a favorite for this style of edit.
Sung Jin Woo (Solo Leveling) — his quiet, understated reactions to increasingly absurd power scaling are a near-perfect match for the format.
Agamemnon — another recurring pick in the same wave of "overpowered and unbothered" character edits.

sections: The common thread across all four: the character does something remarkable and the edit deliberately underplays it, which is exactly what "farming aura" means outside of anime too.
How this connects to the original meme

The anime edits and the original aura farming meme (which started with a real video of a kid dancing on a canoe in Indonesia) share the same rulebook: reacting with zero visible effort reads as more impressive than any reaction at all. Anime just gave the internet a huge, pre-existing library of clips that already fit that description.
faq: Why is Piccolo associated with aura farming?

Because his character is defined by staying calm and saying little even in extreme situations, which matches the aura farming template of doing something impressive without any visible effort or reaction.
What other characters show up in aura farming edits?
Gojo Satoru from Jujutsu Kaisen, Sung Jin Woo from Solo Leveling, and Agamemnon are the most common besides Piccolo, all for the same reason: calm confidence in the face of overwhelming power.
Is aura farming only an anime thing?
No, it started with a real video, not an anime clip. Anime characters became a popular subject for the edits afterward because they fit the format so well.

articles.title: How to Aura Farm: A Practical Guide | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: How to aura farm in real life: the step-by-step, the most common mistakes that cost you aura, and how to practice without overthinking it.
articles.answer: Aura farming in practice comes down to timing and silence: react calmly, don't explain what you did, and never look for a reaction from anyone. Break any of those three rules and you lose the aura instantly, no matter how impressive the original action was.
sections: The step-by-step
There's no real technique here — it's a habit you build. These are the four steps that show up in basically every clip:

ul: Let the moment happen. You can't plan aura farming in advance — the whole point is that the reaction looks natural.
React a beat late. An instant reaction reads as anxious. A short pause before you respond reads as control.
Don't look around afterward. The urge to check if anyone noticed is what kills the aura fastest. Keep moving like nothing happened.
Don't talk about it. If someone asks, say as little as possible. Explaining your own move is the quickest way to zero it out.

sections: Mistakes that cost you aura

ul: Sending a follow-up message explaining the first one.
Asking “did you see that?” after doing something cool.
Laughing at your own joke before you finish telling it.
Celebrating out loud over something small.
Asking someone to delete a photo of you — that guarantees more people see it.

faq: Can you actually practice aura farming on purpose?
Only up to a point — the core rule is that announcing you're aura farming cancels it out. The most you can practice is the habit of not explaining yourself and not checking for a reaction.
What's the single biggest mistake beginners make?
Celebrating. The most natural reaction after doing something well is to smile or comment on it — and that's exactly what zeroes out the aura in this meme.

articles.title: Aura Battles: What They Are, Where They Happen, How to Win | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: What an aura battle (or aura farming competition) actually is, where they've happened in real life, the unwritten rules, and how to actually win one.
articles.answer: An aura battle (also called an aura farming competition) is an informal face-off where two or more people take turns posing, making an entrance, or pulling off a move with total seriousness, and whoever's watching decides on the spot who has more aura. It started as something filmed for TikTok and ended up spilling into real life — actual aura battles have already happened in shopping malls, plazas, and schoolyards in multiple countries.
sections: What an aura battle actually is

It's the group, in-person version of the meme: instead of one person calmly reacting to an everyday situation, two or more people take turns doing poses, entrances, or choreographed moves, almost always with epic music playing. There's no real scoring or judge — whoever's watching decides on the spot, out loud, who walked away with more aura.

There's no organization behind it. The format started in schools and spread to the street as a game, then went viral on TikTok in 2025: someone posts a flyer with a time and place, people show up, and the round happens right there.
Where aura battles actually happen

Real aura battles have already been covered by news outlets in several cities. In Valencia, Spain, a group of teens organized one in a shopping mall and ended up moving to a nearby park after security broke it up; similar gatherings were reported in A Coruña. In Mexico, early videos showed friends putting together spontaneous battles of their own.
The pattern repeats everywhere: someone posts a TikTok flyer with a location and time, word spreads, and the actual event ends up smaller — and more improvised — than the final video suggests.
The unwritten rules
Nobody wrote these down anywhere, but almost every aura battle ends up following the same ones:

ul: Whoever laughs first during their own entrance loses automatically.
Explaining the pose afterward — "no wait, I was doing this because..." — is also an instant loss.
Epic background music isn't required, but it helps a lot.
The crowd votes out loud, by acclaim. Whoever shouts loudest wins the tiebreak.
Going in without any seriousness (clowning around on purpose) disqualifies you — the joke only works if you commit to it.

sections: How to win an aura battle
Winning has less to do with how elaborate your pose is and more to do with how little you seem to care about the outcome. A few things that show up in the battles that go well:

ul: Go in with something simple and commit to it completely. A complex pose that falls apart loses to a simple one held with total confidence.
Don't look for the crowd's reaction while you're posing. Checking whether people are filming or laughing costs you points instantly.
Hold something back for last. If everyone's doing the same thing, whoever closes with a variation wins the tiebreak.
If it goes wrong, don't fix it on the spot. Playing off a mistake like it was intentional gives you more aura than not messing up at all.

sections: The underlying rule is the same one from the original meme: whoever explains themselves, loses.
The online version: aura duels

Getting people together in person isn't always possible — that's where the site's aura duels come in as the online version of the exact same idea: instead of a crowd gathered in a park, anyone can jump in and vote on who has more aura, with the ranking updating live as votes come in.

There are three versions: everyday archetypes (who has more aura, the person who's always late or the one who replies way too fast?), historical figures (Cleopatra vs. Einstein), and celebrities. In all three, the winner of each duel steals points from the loser, exactly like a real battle — except the scoreboard actually sticks around.
faq: What is an aura battle?

It's an informal face-off where two or more people take turns posing or making an entrance with total seriousness, and the crowd watching decides on the spot who has more aura. There's no official organization or real scoring.
Where do aura battles happen?

They started as TikTok videos, but real ones have already happened in public — shopping malls, plazas, schoolyards. They're organized by posting a flyer with a time and place and letting people show up.
How do you win an aura battle?

By going in with something simple but fully committing to it, not looking for the crowd's reaction while you pose, and never explaining yourself if something goes wrong. Whoever laughs first or justifies themselves loses automatically.
Is there an official aura battle organization?
No. It's an informal format that started in schools and went viral on TikTok in 2025. Every group makes up its own rules on the spot.
Can you do an aura battle online?
Yes. The site's aura duels work just like an in-person battle, but with real votes from anyone who joins in: you pick which of two options has more aura, and the ranking moves live with every vote.

articles.title: Aura Farming Glossary: Every Term Explained | Farmear Aura
articles.desc: Aura farming, aura points, negative aura, aura championship, 6-7, rizz: the complete glossary of meme terms, explained one by one.
articles.answer: This aura farming glossary collects and explains every term from the meme: from "aura farming" and "aura points" to the site's own modes, the aura championship, and the concepts it gets mixed up with, like "6-7" or "rizz".
sections: Core terms

dl: Aura farming
Building up charisma on purpose through actions that look effortless. The central verb of the whole meme: reacting well without explaining yourself or seeking anyone's approval.
Aura points
A fictional, made-up unit for measuring an action. There's no official scale — the convention is round, exaggerated numbers, both for gains and losses.
Having aura
Reacting well to a tough situation without showing effort or asking for anyone's reaction. The meme's ideal state.
Losing aura
The opposite of having aura: over-explaining, reacting badly, or fishing for approval after something happens.
Negative aura
A running total below zero after an embarrassing moment. Used as a joke, never seriously.
Aura bankruptcy
Extreme negative aura, when someone chains several mistakes together in a short time.
Aura farming kid
The internet nickname for Rayyan Arkan Dikha, the Indonesian kid from the canoe whose 2025 video started the meme.
Aura edits
Short videos that pair an everyday moment or an anime scene with epic music, framing calm or power as maximum effortlessness.
Infinite aura
An exaggeration of the concept describing someone (real or fictional) who never loses composure, as in the joke that certain athletes have infinite aura.

sections: Modes and formats on this site

dl: Gamer Mode
One of the site's three aura calculator modes, covering matches, voice chat, and win streaks.
School Mode
The calculator's school-themed mode: exams, presentations, hallways.
Party & Crush Mode
The mode for nights out and texts with a crush: the blue double check, 2 am messages, dancing at a party.
Aura championship
An informal pose-and-entrance contest that started in schools and went viral on TikTok in 2025. Whoever's watching decides who has more aura, on the spot and out loud.
Aura duel / aura battle
A one-on-one vote between two options — everyday archetypes, historical figures, or celebrities — where the winner steals aura points from the loser. The ranking updates live with every vote.
Gamer aura / football aura / anime aura
Themed variants of the same concept applied to gaming, football, and anime, each with its own test on the site.

sections: Related terms (and what they aren't)

dl: 6-7 / six seven
A different meme that circulated around the same time as aura farming and showed up in the same videos. It comes from a song and has no fixed meaning — it has no real connection to aura farming.
Rizz
A related but distinct meme: short for "charisma," and specifically about the ability to attract or flirt. Aura farming is broader — it applies to any situation, not just romantic ones.
Esoteric aura / aura colors
A supposed energy field with colors and spiritual meanings. It has no connection to TikTok's aura, which is purely a metaphor for charisma.
Main character energy
A related English-language phrase: acting like you're the protagonist of your own life. It overlaps partly with "having aura," but it's more about a general attitude than one specific reaction.

faq: Is aura farming the same as having rizz?
Not exactly. Both measure a form of charisma, but rizz is specifically about attracting or flirting, while aura farming applies to any everyday situation, not just romantic ones.
Where do all these terms come from?
Most of them started on TikTok in 2025, from Rayyan Arkan Dikha's viral video, and kept getting added as the meme spread to gaming, football, anime, and school life.
Is there an official list of aura farming terms?
There's no official organization behind any of this. This page collects the meme's most-used terms and gets updated as new ones show up.

articles.answer: Aura memes are the funniest side of the whole "aura farming" phenomenon: points you gain and lose like a video game, anime characters that became shorthand for effortless charisma, and even an NFL tight end recreating a viral dance on his own TikTok. Here are the ones that went the most viral, with real origins and sources.
sections: Aura Points: how many did you lose today?

The most viral format of all started on May 1, 2024, when TikToker @aidan2funny posted the first video using the "How many aura points did I lose when..." format, describing an embarrassing situation with a made-up score. By mid-May it exploded: @kerem.as45's "school edition" passed 26 million views, and @d1edger19's video about the worst ways to lose points at school hit 14.6 million.

The funny part is almost nobody gains points in these videos — the joke is in losing them, turning everyday micro-embarrassments (stuttering, crying over a crush, asking for attention) into a quantifiable loss. It's the same joke behind our own aura counter, which adds or subtracts random amounts with their own made-up reason.

On November 29, 2024, someone posted a Dragon Ball Super clip to Instagram showing Piccolo standing with his arms crossed while everyone around him panicked, captioned "aura farming till death." In April 2025, a clip went viral of streamer IShowSpeed asking a girl on the street if she knew his name; she answered with his real name, "Darren Watkins Jr.," and shrugged like it was nothing. Almost a year later, in March 2026, someone re-edited that same clip with a crown and the caption "pure aura," and the new edit passed 840,000 views in two months.
It's a good example of how a lot of this meme works: an old clip can go viral all over again years later, with a new edit, if it fits the moment's aesthetic.

sections: The American version: Travis Kelce farms the aura himself

On July 2, 2025, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce posted a TikTok recreating the viral Indonesian "boat kid" dance (the original clip the whole aura farming meme is built on), set to "Young Black & Rich" by Melly Mike, captioned "The aura has been farmed #indonesia #boatkid #aurafarming." It passed 14 million views. The same week, USMNT midfielder Diego Luna did the identical dance live on the pitch after scoring in a Gold Cup semifinal win over Guatemala — both moments are widely cited as the trend's breakout into mainstream American sports culture.
It's one of the clearest real-world proof points that this meme isn't just an online joke anymore — same story our own aura battles map is tracking as it keeps happening in person.

faq: What does "aura meme" mean?

It's how a lot of people search for the aura-farming meme phenomenon: videos, edits, or images that use the joke of "having aura" (effortless charisma) or "losing aura" (embarrassment) as the basis for the humor.
Who invented the aura points meme?

The "how many aura points did I lose when...?" format was first posted by TikToker @aidan2funny on May 1, 2024. It went massively viral about two weeks later, with school-themed versions passing 25 million views.
Why are there so many anime character memes?

Because the aura-farming format rewards reacting to something overwhelming with total calm, and several anime characters (Piccolo leading the pack) have scenes built exactly like that. It was existing content that happened to fit the joke perfectly.
Do these memes have anything to do with the esoteric "aura colors" reading?

No. The esoteric reading is about a supposed energy field with colors and spiritual meanings. The memes in this piece are something else entirely: they use "aura" as a stand-in for charisma, with no connection to that tradition.
Is "aura farming" the same thing as an "aura meme"?

They're related but not identical. Aura farming is the broader concept, including the in-person battles that have already happened in several countries. The aura memes in this piece are specifically the viral formats that started online around that same idea.
